14620:
A sinew is a tough, strong, cord-like tissue inside your body that connects a muscle to a bone. The scientific word for it is a tendon, and sinew and tendon mean exactly the same thing — sinew is just the older, more literary word.

Think of it this way: your muscles are what generate force (like an engine), and your bones are the frame that moves (like wheels). But something has to physically link the engine to the wheels so the power can transfer. That link is the sinew. When your muscle contracts and pulls, it is the sinew that carries that pull all the way to the bone, making your limb move.

If you have ever handled a raw chicken leg, you have seen sinew — those pale, whitish, stringy threads that are extremely hard to cut through and feel almost like thin ropes. That toughness is the whole point. Sinews must bear enormous tension and force every single time a muscle contracts, so they are built to be nearly indestructible.

Key physical qualities of a sinew:

  • Very tough and fibrous (made of densely packed collagen fibers)
  • Flexible, but does not stretch much — it transmits force efficiently rather than absorbing it like elastic
  • Whitish or silvery in appearance
  • Cord-like or strap-like in shape

This is where the word gets much richer. Because sinews are literally the things that hold the body together and give it the power to act, the word has been extended to mean anything that serves as the core source of strength, power, or binding force — in a person, an organization, or a system.

There are two main figurative uses:

1. Raw physical strength or muscular power in a person

When someone talks about a person's sinews, they often mean their muscular strength in a vivid, almost poetic way — the raw physical power that their body is capable of producing.

"He stretched his sinews and hurled the boulder aside."

Here, "sinews" paints a picture of taut, straining muscles and physical might — far more visceral and powerful than simply saying "he used his strength."

2. The essential driving force or resource behind something

This is the most commonly seen figurative use in serious writing. A sinew of something means the vital ingredient that makes it work, sustains it, or gives it power — just as a sinew in the body enables action.

"Discipline is the sinew of any great team."
"Money is the sinew of industry."

The famous phrase "the sinews of war" has been used for centuries to mean the financial resources and material supplies that make a war effort possible. The idea is that an army without money and supplies is like a body without sinews — it simply cannot move or act.

The plural form, sinews, carries a slightly broader feel than the singular. It can refer to:

  • Multiple tendons collectively
  • The overall muscular and physical constitution of a person or creature
  • Multiple foundational strengths of a system or institution

"The sinews of the nation's economy had been strained by years of mismanagement."
Putting It All Together — Example Sentences

These sentences show the full range of how "sinew" is used:

Literal (body)"He tore a sinew in his knee during the fall."
Literal (animal/meat)"She cut through the tough sinew of the joint before cooking it."
Figurative (personal strength)"Every sinew of his body strained as he climbed the wall."
Figurative (institutional strength)"Trust is the sinew that holds a community together."
Figurative (resources/power)"Trade routes were the sinews of the ancient empire."
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you remember just one thing about this word: a sinew is what transfers force and holds things together — literally inside the body as a tendon, and figuratively as whatever core resource or quality powers and binds something larger. It always carries a sense of toughness, strength, and essential connection.
14621:
A sinew is a tendon — the tough, cord-like tissue inside your body that connects muscle to bone. When you say someone or something is sinewy, you are saying they have the qualities of that tissue: lean, tough, strong, and visibly muscular — without being soft, puffy, or bulky.

It is the kind of strength that looks worked for and lived in, not inflated.

When used to describe a person or animal, sinewy means:

  • The muscles are lean and defined, not hidden under fat or puffed up like a balloon.
  • The body looks tight and ropey — you can almost see the muscles and tendons working under the skin, like cables pulling under a surface.
  • It suggests toughness and endurance, not just size.

Think of a long-distance runner, a rock climber, a seasoned blacksmith, or a wild horse. They are not enormous or bulky — but every part of them is hard, useful muscle. There is no excess. That is sinewy.

Compare this to a bodybuilder, whose muscles are large and rounded. A bodybuilder is muscular or brawny. A marathon runner, however, is sinewy — lean, striated, tough as rope.

Examples in sentences:

  • His arms were sinewy from years of pulling nets out of the sea.
  • The old farmer was small but sinewy, and he worked harder than men half his age.
  • The greyhound's sinewy body was built for nothing but pure speed.

This contrast is very important for remembering the word:

Instead of...Sinewy means...
Soft, doughy, or flabbyLean and hard
Puffy or inflated (like a bodybuilder)Tight and ropey, like cable
Weak or thinStrong and capable
Hidden or invisible muscleClearly defined, visible muscle

Sinewy is not soft or flabby. It is not the inflated, rounded look of someone purely focused on size. And it is not just "thin" or "skinny" — a skinny person may have no muscle at all. A sinewy person is genuinely, functionally strong — just without the bulk.

This is where the word becomes especially interesting and powerful.

When "sinewy" is applied to writing, speech, or arguments, it carries the same idea over from the body: strong, lean, and without unnecessary flab. Sinewy writing is:

  • Direct and powerful — it gets to the point without wasting words.
  • Tight and forceful — every sentence does real work, like a muscle doing its job.
  • Hard to dismiss or ignore — it has real strength behind it.

Just as a sinewy body has no excess fat, sinewy prose has no excess words.

Ernest Hemingway's writing is a classic example people describe as sinewy — short, stripped-back sentences that hit hard precisely because they carry no fluff. A sinewy argument is one that is logical, tight, and difficult to argue against.

Examples in sentences:

  • The lawyer made a sinewy case — every point was precise, and there was nothing loose to pick apart.
  • Her writing style was sinewy: short sentences, strong verbs, no decoration.
  • The speech was not poetic or flowery, but it was sinewy and convincing.
A Less Common Use (Food and Meat)

When describing meat or food, sinewy simply means tough and stringy — containing actual sinew (tendons). This is almost always a negative quality in this context.

  • The steak was overcooked and sinewy — almost impossible to chew.

This usage is the most literal of all: the meat actually contains tough, fibrous tendons.
One Sentence to Capture It All

Sinewy means lean and visibly tough-strong — whether describing a person's muscles, an animal's body, or the way a piece of writing or an argument is built: no excess, no softness, just hard, functional, cord-like strength.
Think of the word sinew (a tough tendon) sitting right inside sinewy. Whenever you see the word, picture a tendon — tough, lean, ropey, built for pulling hard. That image is the meaning.
14622:
To singe something means to burn it very lightly on the surface — just enough to scorch the outermost layer, but not enough to set it on fire, burn it through, or destroy it. Think of it as the gentlest possible form of burning: a quick, shallow, surface-level encounter with heat or flame.

The key idea is incompleteness. Something that has been singed hasn't truly burned — it has only barely burned. The damage stays on the outside. The object survives.
What Singed Things Look Like and Smell Like

When something is singed, you typically see:

  • A slight discolouration — the surface turns brown, yellow, or black at the edges
  • Curling, crisping, or shrivelling of the affected area (especially with hair or fabric)
  • Sometimes a small amount of smoke

You also typically smell it — singed hair, singed cloth, singed feathers all produce a distinctive, unpleasant burning odour. In fact, that smell is often the first clue that something has been singed.

Hair — This is probably the most common context for the word.

"She leaned too close to the birthday candles and singed the ends of her hair."

The tips of her hair caught a brief flash of heat. They didn't go up in flames — they just shrivelled and burned slightly at the very ends.

"He singed his eyebrows while lighting the gas stove."

A sudden flare of flame briefly touched his eyebrows. They weren't gone — just slightly burned and curled.

Fabric and clothing

"The iron was too hot, and she singed the collar of his white shirt."

The iron sat a moment too long and scorched just the surface of the fabric — leaving a brown mark, but not burning a hole through it.

Food

"The chef accidentally singed the edges of the flatbread."

The bread's edges got a little charred and darkened, but the bread itself was still edible.

Feathers and fur

"The farmer singed the chicken over an open flame to remove the last fine feathers."

This is actually a traditional technique — passing poultry briefly over fire to burn off the tiny pin-feathers left after plucking. It doesn't cook the bird; it only removes the surface feathers.

Plants and grass

"The wildfire singed the trees at the edge of the field but didn't burn them down."

The trees were touched by the heat and flame — their outer bark and leaves slightly scorched — but they were still standing.

The word "singe" always carries the idea that the burning is minor and surface-level. This is what separates it from stronger words like burn, scorch, and char.

Think of it as a scale of intensity:

  • Singe → the lightest touch of heat; only the very surface is affected; the object is basically intact
  • Scorch → a bit more intense; leaves a noticeable brown or black mark; the word can sometimes be used interchangeably with singe, but typically implies slightly more damage
  • Char → the surface turns black and crumbles into carbon; clearly damaged
  • Burn → the broadest and most general word; can be light or severe; can go deep

So if someone singed their fingers, they're fine — it was brief and barely hurt. If someone burned their fingers, that could mean anything from a minor irritation to a serious injury.
How It Happens: Usually Briefly and Accidentally

Singes usually happen because of:

  • A moment's carelessness near an open flame (a candle, a gas burner, a bonfire)
  • Brief contact with something intensely hot
  • A sudden flare or spark

It's rarely intentional (except in the case of removing feathers from poultry, as mentioned above). Most of the time, someone singed something because they weren't being careful enough.
Using the Word in Different Forms

The verb changes form like this:

  • Present: "She singes the edges of the meat to seal in the juices." (rare in this form; more naturally used in past tense)
  • Past tense: "He singed his sleeve on the campfire."
  • Present participle: "She was singeing the fabric without realising it." (Notice: it's spelled "singeing," not "singing" — the 'e' is kept deliberately to avoid confusion.)
  • Past participle: "The singed curtains had to be replaced."

Like many physical words, "singe" can be used figuratively — meaning to slightly damage something non-physical, without destroying it.

"The scandal singed his reputation, but he recovered."

His reputation wasn't ruined — it was just lightly damaged, the way a surface is lightly burned. He came out the other side still intact.

"Her cruel remark singed his confidence."

It hurt — it left a mark — but it didn't break him entirely.

This figurative use works precisely because of what the word literally means: a surface-level wound that falls short of destruction.
To singe is to burn something very lightly and superficially — just the outer surface — without truly destroying it, typically by brief or accidental contact with heat or flame.
14623: "Singular" means relating to just one. Almost every meaning of this word grows from that single seed. Think of it as the opposite of "many" or "multiple." Whenever you see "singular," your brain should first think: one — standing apart from the rest.
Meaning 1: Grammar — "One, Not Many"

In grammar, "singular" simply means that a word refers to one person, place, thing, or idea — as opposed to plural, which means more than one.

  • "Cat" is singular. "Cats" is plural.
  • "The child is happy" — child is singular. "The children are happy" — children is plural.
  • "He runs" — he is singular, so the verb takes its singular form.

This is the most clear-cut use of the word. When a grammar teacher says "use the singular form," they simply mean: treat this as if you are talking about one thing.
Meaning 2: Exceptional — "Remarkably Outstanding"

Outside grammar, "singular" often means so extraordinary that it stands in a class of its own. There is a quiet suggestion of uniqueness built into this meaning — the thing being described is not just good, it is one of a kind good.

  • "She has a singular talent for music." → Her talent is not merely impressive — it is so outstanding it is almost in its own league.
  • "He showed singular courage during the crisis." → A level of courage that is hard to find in others.
  • "This was a singular moment in history." → A moment so remarkable it stands completely alone.

The tone here is one of high praise. This is a compliment that lifts the thing being described above the ordinary crowd. It is the kind of word you find in formal writing, literary prose, or when someone wants to say "impressive" but with more weight and elegance.
Meaning 3: Strange or Peculiar — "Noticeably Odd"

"Singular" can also describe something that is unusual in a curious or odd way — not necessarily bad or great, but definitely noticeable and out of the ordinary. It makes you raise an eyebrow.

  • "He had a singular habit of humming to himself while working." → A quirky, peculiar habit.
  • "There was something singular about the silence in that room." → An unusual, hard-to-explain quality.
  • "She gave him a singular look." → A strange, unreadable look.

Think of this as a polite, formal way of saying "odd, but in a way worth noticing." It does not mean bad — just distinctly different from the norm. A writer might choose "singular" over "weird" because it sounds more thoughtful and less dismissive.
Meaning 4: Unique — "One of Its Kind"

Sometimes "singular" simply means there is nothing else quite like it — it is truly one of a kind.

  • "This is a singular opportunity — don't let it pass." → A once-in-a-lifetime chance, unrepeatable.
  • "She occupies a singular place in the history of science." → A position no one else holds.

This meaning overlaps with Meaning 2 (exceptional), but the focus here shifts slightly. The emphasis is on rarity and uniqueness rather than just greatness. Something can be singularly strange just as easily as it can be singularly brilliant. The point is: there is only one like it.
Meaning 5: Mathematics and Technical Fields — "A Special, Exceptional Point"

In mathematics, "singular" describes something that behaves in an exceptional or abnormal way at a specific point — usually where normal rules break down.

  • A singular matrix is a matrix that has no inverse (because its determinant is zero). It is "singular" in the sense that it is an exception to how most matrices behave.
  • A singular point in calculus is a point on a curve or graph where the function behaves unusually — perhaps it is undefined there, or the curve has a sharp corner or a cusp.

In physics, you may have heard of a singularity — such as inside a black hole — which is a point where normal physical laws break down completely. This is the same idea: a singular, exceptional, rule-breaking point.

You do not need to master this technical sense unless you study mathematics or physics, but it is good to know it exists.
How to Tell Which Meaning is Being Used

Context is your guide every time:

  • In a grammar textbook → it means "one, not plural."
  • In formal or literary writing, with a positive tone → it means "exceptional, remarkable."
  • With a slightly raised-eyebrow or curious tone → it means "peculiar, odd."
  • Emphasizing rarity or one-of-a-kindness → it means "unique."
  • In a mathematics or science context → it means "behaving abnormally at a specific point."
The Common Thread Across All Meanings

Every single meaning of "singular" shares one underlying idea:

Standing apart from the many.

Whether it is one noun in grammar, one extraordinary person, one odd habit, one unrepeatable opportunity, or one abnormal point in mathematics — "singular" always points to something that does not blend in. It singles itself out from everything around it. That is why the word itself contains the idea of singleness at its heart.
How "Singular" Differs from Similar Words

Unique means one of a kind — no more, no less. "Singular" can mean the same, but it also carries the additional flavors of "exceptional" or "peculiar." Unique is factual and neutral; singular is more expressive.

Peculiar leans entirely into strangeness, and can sound somewhat negative. "Singular" in its strange-meaning is subtler, more formal, and more neutral in judgment.

Exceptional means unusually good. "Singular" is similar, but adds the feel of standing completely alone — not just above average, but in its own category altogether.

Extraordinary means beyond the ordinary. "Singular" is similar, but quieter and more literary in tone.
Related Word Forms

• Singularly (adverb): "She was singularly gifted." → Means exceptionally, remarkably. Used to intensify a quality.
  • Singularity (noun): The state or quality of being singular — uniqueness, remarkableness, or in science/math, an exceptional point where normal rules break down.
A Quick Summary

UseWhat it means

"Singular" means one of five related things: (1) referring to one thing in grammar, (2) exceptionally outstanding, (3) strangely peculiar, (4) one of a kind, or (5) mathematically abnormal at a specific point. All five meanings circle back to the same idea — something that stands apart, alone, and distinct from everything else around it.
14624:
A singularity is a point — a moment, a location, or a condition — that is so extreme, so utterly unlike everything around it, that normal rules stop working there. It is the one point where everything breaks.

Think of it this way: imagine a smooth road that suddenly drops into a bottomless pit. The road behaves normally everywhere — you can measure it, drive on it, predict what comes next. But right at that pit? All normal rules collapse. That pit is a singularity.

This core idea plays out across different fields in different but related ways.
Meaning 1: A Unique or Remarkable Quality (General Use)

In everyday and literary language, a singularity is simply a quality or feature that makes something stand completely alone — something so distinctive that nothing else quite matches it.

If someone says "one of the singularities of her personality was her ability to be blunt without being unkind," they mean that this quality was so unusual and characteristic of her that it set her apart from everyone else. It was hers alone.

This meaning is rare in modern casual speech, but you will encounter it in older writing and formal contexts. The key idea is extreme uniqueness — not just different, but one-of-a-kind.

In mathematics, a singularity is a point where a mathematical function breaks down — where it becomes undefined or shoots off to infinity.

Here's the simplest example: take the function 1/x. If x = 2, the answer is 0.5. If x = 0.1, the answer is 10. If x = 0.001, the answer is 1,000. As x gets closer and closer to zero, the answer explodes toward infinity. At x = 0 exactly, the function doesn't give you any meaningful number at all — it's undefined. That point, x = 0, is a singularity.

The function works perfectly everywhere else. You can calculate, predict, and reason about it normally. But right at that one point, the mathematics itself ceases to function. It hits a wall.

This is the technical foundation that all other uses of "singularity" borrow from.

In physics — especially in Einstein's theory of general relativity — a singularity is a point in space (or in the history of the universe) where matter is compressed into infinite density, and where our known laws of physics completely break down.

There are two famous examples:

The center of a black hole. A black hole forms when a massive star collapses under its own gravity. As you go deeper into a black hole, gravity gets stronger and stronger, matter gets packed more and more densely. At the very center, our equations predict infinite density — a point of zero volume containing enormous mass. This is the singularity. We call it a singularity not because we know exactly what is there, but because our best physical equations stop giving sensible answers at that point. The math breaks, just as 1/x breaks at zero.

The Big Bang. If you trace the universe backward in time — it was smaller yesterday than today, smaller a million years ago than yesterday — you eventually reach a point, roughly 13.8 billion years ago, where all the matter and energy in the entire universe was compressed into an inconceivably small, unimaginably hot and dense state. That origin point is also called a singularity. Time itself, as we understand it, may not have existed before it. Our physics cannot describe what was "before" or "inside" this point — it's the ultimate edge of what our equations can reach.

The important thing to understand is that a physical singularity isn't just an extreme condition — it is the point where the very tools we use to understand the universe (mathematics, physics, causality) stop functioning. Beyond it, we have no reliable map.

This is a more recent and very widely discussed meaning, especially in conversations about artificial intelligence and the future.

The Technological Singularity refers to a hypothetical future point at which artificial intelligence surpasses human intelligence, triggering a runaway chain of self-improvement and change so rapid and profound that the future becomes fundamentally unpredictable and incomprehensible to us from our current vantage point.

The logic goes like this: today, humans are the smartest things that exist. We design our tools, including our AI. But imagine an AI that becomes smarter than any human — it could then design a smarter AI than itself, which could design an even smarter one, and so on, in a cycle that accelerates faster and faster. At some point, the pace of change would become so extreme that we would have no way to predict what comes after, just as you cannot see beyond the event horizon of a black hole.

The word "singularity" is used here deliberately, borrowing from the mathematical and physical meanings: it is the point beyond which our current models, predictions, and understanding cannot reach. Just as a black hole singularity is where physics breaks down, the technological singularity is where human foresight breaks down.

The concept is associated with thinkers like Vernor Vinge (who formalized it) and Ray Kurzweil (who made it widely known and predicted it would occur around 2045). It is important to note that the Technological Singularity is a hypothesis, not an established fact — it is a subject of serious intellectual debate, not a confirmed prediction. Some scientists and thinkers find it compelling; others argue that intelligence doesn't self-amplify so neatly, or that the analogy to mathematical singularities is too loose to be meaningful.

All uses of "singularity" share the same underlying structure:

A single, extreme point that is utterly unlike everything around it, and at which normal rules — whether mathematical, physical, social, or intellectual — cease to apply.

Whether it is a unique personality trait, a point where an equation explodes to infinity, the collapsed core of a dead star, the birth-moment of the universe, or a hypothetical future of uncontrollable AI growth — in every case, a singularity is the one place where the usual framework fails to hold, and something categorically different takes over.

That is why the word carries a sense of both awe and unease. It marks the edge of what we can fully understand or predict.
14625:
"Sinister" describes something that is, or strongly appears to be, evil, threatening, or deeply wrong — especially in a dark, hidden, or secretive way. It carries the idea that something malevolent (meaning: wishing or intending harm) is lurking, either beneath the surface or right in plain view.

A useful way to feel the word: imagine walking into a room and sensing immediately that something is not just uncomfortable, but darkly, dangerously wrong — the kind of wrongness that goes beyond "odd" or "creepy" into something genuinely evil. That feeling, and whatever is causing it, is sinister.

Sinister works in two closely related ways, and it often carries both at once.

The first is about appearance — something that looks or feels threatening and evil, even before you can prove it. The second is about reality — something that actually is evil, harmful, or criminal in its nature or intent.

What makes sinister special is that it very often combines both: something sinister both looks wrong and is wrong.

When describing appearance (looks or feels sinister):

  • "There was something sinister about the stranger's smile — it never quite reached his eyes."
  • "The empty factory looked sinister in the middle of the night."
  • "She felt a sinister presence as soon as she entered the building."

When describing reality (actually is sinister):

  • "The investigation uncovered a sinister plot to steal money from thousands of ordinary people."
  • "He had sinister intentions when he befriended the elderly woman."
  • "The company's cheerful advertising concealed a sinister practice of exploiting its workers."
The tone and feel of the word

Sinister is a strong word. It is not mild or casual. When you call something sinister, you are saying it is not simply odd, suspicious, or uncomfortable — you are saying it has the quality of genuine evil or serious, dangerous threat.

Crucially, sinister almost always carries a sense of something hidden or concealed. A sinister smile looks pleasant on the outside but hides something dark underneath. A sinister plan appears normal on the surface but conceals a harmful purpose. This is the word's great power: it captures not just evil, but disguised or lurking evil.

Very strong. Think of it on a rising scale:

Odd → Suspicious → Shady → Threatening → Sinister → Evil

Sinister sits near the extreme end, close to outright evil. It is not the right word for everyday problems, minor discomfort, or simple strangeness. Use it when something carries a genuinely dark, threatening, or malevolent quality.

Not the same as "scary" or "spooky." A horror movie can be scary. A ghost story can be spooky. Neither is necessarily sinister. Sinister specifically implies evil intent or evil nature — not just fear or fright.

Not the same as "suspicious." Suspicious means something raises doubts or questions. Sinister goes much further and deeper — it means something is genuinely dark or evil in its character.

Not the same as "gloomy" or "dark." A rainy day, a sad mood, or a grim situation is not sinister. Sinister always requires that core element of malevolence — actual or strongly implied evil.

Sinister pairs naturally and frequently with certain words. Knowing these will help you recognize and use it confidently:

Sinister motives / sinister intentions — someone has evil or harmful plans, often kept secret.

A sinister plot / scheme — a plan that is both evil and deliberately hidden from others.

A sinister figure — a person who looks or actually is threatening and evil in nature.

A sinister smile / look / expression — a facial expression that appears normal but conceals something dark.

A sinister atmosphere / presence — a place or general feeling that radiates a sense of evil or danger.

Sinister is fully at home in both formal and informal contexts. You will encounter it in literature, journalism, legal language, and film descriptions. In casual conversation, people more often reach for words like "creepy," "shady," or "sketchy" — but sinister is absolutely understood and used in everyday speech, particularly when a person wants to be precise and emphatic about the darkness of something.
Sinister means: genuinely evil, darkly threatening, or deeply wrong — especially in a way that is hidden, concealed, or lurking beneath the surface.
14626: A sinking feeling is a sudden, unpleasant physical sensation — felt mostly in your stomach or chest — that happens the moment you realize something is wrong, something bad is about to happen, or that a situation is worse than you hoped. It is a mix of dread, alarm, and helplessness all arriving at once, in your body, not just your mind.

This phrase describes something very real that your body does. When you are alarmed or deeply dismayed, your stomach seems to drop — as if it has fallen downward inside you. You feel hollow, heavy, or empty in your gut. Your chest might tighten. It is the same physical feeling you get on a fast elevator going down, or the first drop of a rollercoaster — except it is caused not by movement, but by a sudden, troubling realization.

This is why the word sinking is used. Something inside you seems to sink downward, like a stone dropped into water.

The phrase captures a very specific moment — the instant when your mind understands something troubling. It is not a slow, creeping worry. It is a sharp, sudden drop in your gut. That split second when your heart seems to fall.

It is also a moment of helplessness — the feeling usually comes when you sense that something bad is already in motion, and there is little or nothing you can do about it.

You feel a sinking feeling when:

  • You suddenly realize you have made a serious mistake. (You send an email and immediately realize you sent it to the wrong person.)
  • You receive unexpected bad news.
  • You sense that a situation is turning out badly.
  • You notice a warning sign that tells you something is very wrong.
  • You remember something important that you forgot to do.
  • You are waiting for a result and something tells you it will be bad.

A sinking feeling is not quite the same as sadness, fear, or anger — though it can contain elements of all three. It is closest to dread mixed with dismay. It is the feeling of:

  • "Oh no."
  • "This is bad."
  • "Something is very wrong."
  • "I already know how this ends, and it isn't good."

It carries a sense that something is collapsing — plans, hopes, expectations — just like a ship that begins to sink.
How to use it in sentences

The phrase is almost always used with the article "a". Here are the natural ways to use it:

Common patterns:

  • have a sinking feeling — She had a sinking feeling the moment she walked in.
  • get a sinking feeling — He got a sinking feeling when he saw the test results.
  • feel a sinking feeling — I felt a sinking feeling in my stomach.
  • with a sinking feeling — With a sinking feeling, she realized her passport was missing.
  • a sinking feeling that... — He had a sinking feeling that he had already failed.

Example sentences:

She had a sinking feeling when she saw the police car parked outside her house.

I got a sinking feeling the moment the interviewer stopped smiling.

He opened the envelope with a sinking feeling — he already knew it was a rejection letter.

With a sinking feeling, she realized she had left her phone on the train.

There was a sinking feeling in his chest when his friend stopped picking up his calls.

Notice that in many sentences, the feeling comes before the full realization is even explained — that is accurate to life. You feel it in your body first, and then your mind catches up.
A sinking feeling vs. a bad feeling

These are related but not the same.

A bad feeling is general — it can mean anything unpleasant.

A sinking feeling is specific — it always involves that physical drop in the stomach, and it always comes from a sudden realization or a strong sense that something is going wrong. It is more vivid, more bodily, and more tied to a particular alarming moment.

A sinking feeling is not a mild discomfort. It is a significant internal jolt. When a writer uses this phrase, they are signaling that a character is experiencing a genuinely alarming or deeply dismaying moment — not a minor inconvenience.

It is also a phrase that feels honest and human. Almost every person has experienced this feeling, so when you use it, readers or listeners instantly understand and connect with what you are describing.

A sinking feeling is the sudden, heavy drop you feel in your gut the moment you realize something has gone wrong or is about to go terribly wrong — a physical sensation of dread, alarm, and helplessness hitting you all at once.
14627:
Sinuosity means the quality or degree of having curves, bends, and winding turns. It describes how curvy or twisting something is — as opposed to being straight.

Think of a river. Some rivers run in a fairly straight line from point A to point B. Others twist and loop and curve dramatically before reaching the same destination. That second river has high sinuosity. The first has low sinuosity. Sinuosity is simply a measure of how much something winds.
The Full Range — From Zero to High

Sinuosity exists on a spectrum. Nothing is simply "sinuous" or "not sinuous" — things can have more or less of it.

A laser beam travelling in a perfectly straight line has essentially zero sinuosity. A gently curving country road has low sinuosity. A mountain switchback road has moderate sinuosity. The Amazon River, which loops back on itself so dramatically that some of its bends nearly form complete circles, has very high sinuosity. A snake slithering through grass is practically a living demonstration of maximum sinuosity.

The word captures not just the fact that something curves, but how much it curves, and how often.
It Describes More Than Just Rivers

While rivers are the most classic example, sinuosity applies to anything that can bend or wind:

A dancer moving fluidly across a stage — her body flowing in graceful, continuous curves — displays sinuosity in her movement. A vine growing up a garden wall, wrapping and spiraling as it climbs, has sinuosity. A piece of calligraphy where the brushstrokes loop and curve beautifully has sinuosity. Even an argument or a piece of prose can be described as having sinuosity — meaning it winds its way to a point rather than going there directly.

So the word is versatile. It works for physical paths, shapes, movements, and even abstract things like thought or narrative.
Sinuosity as a Precise, Measurable Thing

In science — particularly in geography and hydrology (the study of water) — sinuosity isn't just a vague quality. It's a precise, calculable number.

Scientists define it as the ratio of the actual length of a river's path to the straight-line distance between where the river starts and where it ends. The formula looks like this in plain language:

Sinuosity = (Actual winding length of the river) ÷ (Straight-line distance from start to finish)

A perfectly straight river would score exactly 1.0 — because the actual length and the straight-line distance would be the same. The more a river winds, the higher this number climbs above 1.0. A river with heavy, looping bends might score 2.0 or higher, meaning it travels twice the distance it theoretically needs to in order to get from its source to its mouth.

Geographers generally classify rivers like this:

  • Sinuosity of 1.0 to 1.05 → Straight
  • 1.05 to 1.25 → Slightly sinuous
  • 1.25 to 1.5 → Moderately sinuous
  • Above 1.5 → Highly sinuous, or meandering

This makes "sinuosity" one of those rare words that works both in poetry (describing the graceful curve of a valley) and in a scientific paper (complete with a decimal point).

When you use the plural form, "sinuosities," something subtly changes in meaning. The singular "sinuosity" refers to the overall quality of being winding. But the plural "sinuosities" refers to the individual curves and bends themselves.

So you might say:

  • "The sinuosity of the river was remarkable." → You're talking about the river's overall winding nature as a characteristic.
  • "The sinuosities of the river made navigation difficult." → You're talking about the individual bends and loops in the river — each one a sinuosity.

Think of it like the word "beauty." "The beauty of the painting" refers to its overall quality. But "the beauties of the painting" refers to the specific beautiful elements within it. Sinuosity works the same way.

To sharpen the definition further: sinuosity is not the same as roughness or complexity. A rough or jagged path — think of a zigzag — has sharp, angular changes in direction. Sinuosity implies smooth, flowing, curved changes in direction. The bends are graceful, not abrupt. A river meanders sinuously; a mountain path with sharp switchbacks is more angular, though it may still carry some sinuosity in its overall character.

Also, sinuosity is not merely about length. A very long straight road is not sinuous. Sinuosity is specifically about curvature and winding, not distance.

Here are natural, varied examples to show you how the word lives in real usage:

  • "The sinuosity of the Mississippi River is one reason it frequently changes course over centuries."
  • "She moved across the dance floor with a natural sinuosity that held the entire audience captivated."
  • "The architect admired the sinuosity of the staircase — it curved upward like a ribbon rather than climbing in rigid, straight flights."
  • "The essay frustrated its readers with its sinuosity — it wound through so many digressions that its point was nearly lost."
  • "The road's sinuosity made the drive slow but scenic."

If you ever need to recall this word in one clean thought:

Sinuosity is the quality or degree to which something winds, curves, and bends smoothly — rather than travelling in a straight line — and in science, it can be measured precisely as a ratio between actual path length and straight-line distance.

That's the whole word. Everything else — the plural, the contexts, the spectrum — flows from that core idea.
14628:
Sinuous means smoothly and gracefully curved — bending and curving repeatedly, like a snake. Something sinuous is never straight, never jagged or sharp. Instead, it flows through a series of long, smooth, gentle curves, one after the other.

Think of a river seen from above. It doesn't go straight from point A to point B. It curves left, then right, then left again — gliding and bending continuously. That river is sinuous.
The Two Things Sinuous Can Describe

The word works in two main ways:

1. A shape or a path — something that physically curves and bends as you trace along it.

  • A sinuous road through a mountain
  • A sinuous vine crawling up a wall
  • A sinuous coastline full of bays and inlets

2. A movement — the way something moves, flowing in smooth curves rather than stiffly or in a straight line.

  • A dancer's sinuous movements across the stage
  • A cat moving sinuously as it walks
  • A fish weaving sinuously through the water
What Makes It Different from Just "Curved"

This is important. A banana is curved. A rainbow is curved. But we wouldn't usually call them sinuous.

Sinuous implies multiple curves in a flowing sequence. It's not one bend — it's a series of them, connected smoothly. It also carries a sense of elegance and fluidity. Sinuous things move or sit beautifully. There's nothing awkward, stiff, or sudden about them.

So, sinuous = repeatedly curving + smooth + graceful.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

Sinuous carries a slightly poetic, admiring quality. Writers choose this word when they want to describe something with a sense of beauty or captivating complexity. It's not a neutral word. When you call something sinuous, you are almost always suggesting it is visually striking or elegantly formed.

For example:

  • "The road was winding" → plain, factual
  • "The road was sinuous" → the same fact, but now there's a sense of beauty and flow to it

Understanding what the word does not mean helps sharpen your understanding:

  • Not jagged — sharp zigzags are not sinuous. Think of a lightning bolt. That's angular and sudden, not sinuous.
  • Not straight — obviously. Sinuous is the opposite of linear.
  • Not jerky or stiff — sinuous movement is always fluid. A robot walking in a straight line is the opposite of sinuous.
  • Not just "complicated" — something can be complicated without being sinuous. Sinuous complexity specifically refers to a winding, curving kind of complexity.

Think of sinuous as sitting on a spectrum. On one end, you have a straight line. On the other end, you have something wildly tangled or coiled. Sinuous lives in the middle-to-far end of that spectrum — clearly and repeatedly curving, but still with a sense of flow and smoothness, not chaos.

Here are sentences that show the word in different situations:

  • The sinuous river reflected the evening sky as it wound through the plains.

(A river bending gracefully through a landscape)

  • She moved with a sinuous grace that made it impossible to look away.

(Body movement that is smooth and flowing)

  • The architect designed sinuous corridors that curved through the building like a gentle wave.

(The shape of a path or space)

  • The snake glided in a sinuous path through the tall grass.

(A classic image — this is where the word feels most at home)

  • His sinuous argument was hard to follow, twisting in directions you didn't expect.

(A less common but valid use — sinuous can describe logic or writing that winds through many turns, making it complex to follow)

Knowing nearby words helps you understand exactly where sinuous sits:

  • Winding — the most common everyday word. Similar meaning, but far more neutral, with no beauty implied. A winding road is sinuous, but calling it sinuous adds elegance.
  • Serpentine — very close to sinuous, and also evokes the image of a snake. Slightly more formal and vivid. Sinuous feels smoother; serpentine feels more dramatic.
  • Meandering — this usually applies to paths, rivers, or thought patterns that wander slowly and without urgency. Sinuous feels more deliberate and beautiful; meandering feels more aimless.
  • Undulating — describes a wave-like up-and-down motion. Sinuous is more about side-to-side or in-plane curves; undulating is more about rises and dips.
  • Lithe — used for bodies or animals that move with flexible, graceful ease. Sinuous is the broader word; lithe is specifically about the body being supple and agile.
The Single Clearest Image to Lock It In

Close your eyes and picture a cobra rising from a basket, its body curving in flowing S-shapes as it sways. No sharp angles. No jerky movements. Just smooth, continuous, hypnotic curves.

That image is sinuous. Anytime you're unsure whether sinuous fits, ask yourself: does it flow and curve the way a swaying cobra does? If yes, sinuous is likely the right word.
14629:
To sip means to drink something in very small amounts, slowly, one tiny mouthful at a time — instead of taking a big mouthful or drinking quickly.

Think of it this way: when you drink a glass of water because you are thirsty, you probably take several large mouthfuls quickly. But when you pick up a cup of very hot tea, you bring it to your lips and take just a tiny, careful amount. You don't rush. You take a little, pause, and take a little more. That is sipping.

Sipping is not random — people sip for specific reasons, and understanding those reasons will help you use the word naturally.

1. Because the liquid is hot.
This is the most common reason. Hot tea, hot coffee, hot soup — you can't just gulp these down or you'll burn your mouth. So you sip carefully, a tiny amount at a time.

  • She sipped her coffee while it was still steaming.
  • He sipped the hot broth slowly.

2. Because they want to enjoy and savour the taste.
When something tastes wonderful — a fine wine, a good whiskey, a delicious herbal tea — people sip it. They drink it slowly and in small amounts on purpose, to fully experience every drop instead of finishing it too fast.

  • He sipped his red wine, enjoying every drop.
  • She slowly sipped her mango lassi, closing her eyes in pleasure.

3. Because of politeness or social habit.
In formal or relaxed social settings, sipping is considered refined and calm. At a party or a dinner table, people sip their drinks rather than gulping them. It is a way of being unhurried and composed.

  • The guests sipped their cocktails and made pleasant conversation.

4. Because of illness or weakness.
When someone is sick and can't swallow much, or when someone is very weak, they can only manage small amounts of liquid at a time.

  • The doctor told her to sip water throughout the day to stay hydrated.
  • After the surgery, he could only sip apple juice.

5. Because they are distracted or in a relaxed, leisurely mood.
Sometimes people sip not because the drink is special, but simply because they are absorbed in something else — reading a book, watching the rain, having a long conversation — and they drink absentmindedly and slowly.

  • She sat by the window, sipping her chai and watching the street below.
What Makes Sipping Different from Other Drinking Words?

This is important for using the word correctly.

  • Drink is the general, neutral word. It says nothing about speed or amount. You simply take liquid into your mouth and swallow.
  • Gulp / Guzzle means drinking in large amounts, quickly and eagerly — the opposite of sipping. When you are very thirsty and drink fast, you gulp.
  • Slurp means drinking noisily, often considered rude.
  • Sip is specifically about being slow, careful, and taking only a little at a time. It is quiet and controlled.

If someone gulps a cup of tea, they drank it in one or two large mouthfuls, quickly. If someone sips a cup of tea, they spent ten minutes drinking it, a tiny bit at a time.
How the Word Is Used Grammatically

The verb "sip" is flexible. Here are the natural patterns:

sip + something (most common)

  • She sipped her tea.
  • He sipped his morning coffee.

sip + on + something (informal and very common in everyday speech; suggests a relaxed, ongoing action)

  • He was sipping on a cold lemonade.
  • She's been sipping on her hot chocolate all evening.

sip + at + something (suggests a slightly tentative, unhurried, or delicate action — as if testing or enjoying carefully)

  • She sipped at the unfamiliar wine cautiously.
  • He sipped at the soup to check if it was still too hot.

sip + from + something (focuses on the container)

  • She sipped from a tall glass of orange juice.
  • He sipped from the straw.

sip + through + a straw

  • The child sipped his milkshake through a straw.
The Feeling and Tone the Word Carries

"Sip" is not just a mechanical description of a physical action. It carries a certain mood or quality — it suggests something gentle, calm, unhurried, and often pleasurable. When a writer uses "sip," they are painting a picture of someone who is at ease, taking their time, perhaps enjoying a quiet moment.

Compare:

  • He drank his tea. — Plain statement. No particular atmosphere.
  • He sipped his tea. — Immediately gives a sense of calm, leisure, or careful enjoyment.

This is why "sip" appears frequently in descriptions of peaceful scenes, cozy moments, and relaxed conversations.

Though less common, "sip" is sometimes used figuratively to describe absorbing something little by little — not liquid, but information, experience, or pleasure.

  • She sipped the silence of the empty house, grateful for the peace. (She absorbed the quiet slowly and gently, savouring it.)
  • He sipped at the idea, not fully committing to it yet. (He engaged with it tentatively, in small amounts, without diving in.)

This figurative use is found mostly in literary writing and is built entirely on the core idea: taking something in slowly, in small amounts.
A Quick Summary to Anchor It All

To sip = to drink slowly, in very small amounts, one tiny mouthful at a time.

It is done when a drink is hot, when it is special and worth savouring, when you are being polite, when you are unwell, or when you are simply in no hurry. The word carries a tone of gentleness, calm, and care. It is the opposite of gulping or guzzling. You can sip something, sip on something, sip at something, or sip from a container.
